Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — StealC and Amadey: Breaking down infostealers and the cybercrime services that d
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Amadey rundll32 credential/clipper module execution from AppData · [LLM] Amadey loader command handler spawning cmd/PowerShell from AppData self-copy · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Amadey C2 check-in beacon to .php endpoint from AppData-resident process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Amadey rundll32 credential/clipper module execution from AppData AIInstallation High
Hunts rundll32.exe loading Amadey's downloaded credential-stealer (cred64.dll/cred.dll) or clipper (clip64.dll/clip.dll) modules from AppData\Roaming via the exported Main function, corresponding to Amadey command 0x0B (Drop DLL). This is the on-host execution of Amadey's stolen-credential and clipboard-theft plugins. Rationale: Uses the exact Amadey module filenames cred64.dll/clip64.dll loaded via rundll32 from AppData\Roaming (article Table 2 command 0x0B; corroborated by AhnLab ASEC), plus the generic '.dll,Main' export-invocation pattern to catch renamed variants. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/36634/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/amadey-malware-explained-how-the-windows-botnet-loader-and-rat-work • https://research.openanalysis.net/cpp/stl/amadey/loader/config/2022/11/13/amadey.html
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1555 T1115
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LOB software shipping a DLL named cred.dll/clip.dll in AppData loaded via rundll32
  • Third-party clipboard managers registering a clip.dll helper
  • Installer stubs invoking a rundll32 ...,Main export from a per-user AppData path
  • Security/EDR tooling that stages helper DLLs under AppData\Roaming
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName in~ ("Microsoft Corporation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full rundll32 command line and the SHA256/path of the loaded DLL; confirm the DLL sits in AppData\Roaming under a random hex-named folder and is not signed by a known vendor. Check the parent process (Amadey self-copy usually under AppData\Local\Temp). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and parent EXE, and force-reset credentials/session cookies for any account used on that device (cred64.dll harvests stored creds; clip64.dll intercepts clipboard incl. wallet addresses). 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for outbound HTTP to *.php C2 (UC 'Amadey C2 check-in'), other rundll32 loads from AppData, and scheduled tasks / Run keys pointing at the temp self-copy.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cred64.dll","clip64.dll","cred.dll","clip.dll")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "AppData" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.dll\s*,\s*Main")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("cred64.dll","clip64.dll","cred.dll","clip.dll")
    or (CommandLine has "AppData" and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.dll\s*,\s*Main")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Amadey rundll32 Credential and Clipper Module Execution from AppData
id: 8f2c1a4e-3b9d-4e17-9c22-1a2b3c4d5e6f
status: experimental
description: Detects rundll32.exe loading Amadey credential-stealer (cred64.dll/cred.dll) or clipper (clip64.dll/clip.dll) modules dropped to AppData\Roaming, invoking the Main export (Amadey command 0x0B Drop DLL).
references:
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/24/stealc-and-amadey-breaking-down-infostealers-and-the-cybercrime-services-that-deliver-them/
    - https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/36634/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
    - attack.t1218.011
    - attack.t1555
    - attack.t1115
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_img:
        Image|endswith: '\rundll32.exe'
    selection_module:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'cred64.dll'
            - 'clip64.dll'
            - 'cred.dll'
            - 'clip.dll'
    condition: selection_img and selection_module
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate applications loading similarly named DLLs via rundll32
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RunDll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) @CommandLine:(*cred64.dll* OR *clip64.dll* OR *cred.dll* OR *clip.dll*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\rundll32\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/((cred64|clip64|cred|clip)\.dll|\\AppData\\Roaming\\.*\.dll\s*,\s*Main)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=rundll32.exe (Processes.process="*cred64.dll*" OR Processes.process="*clip64.dll*" OR Processes.process="*cred.dll*" OR Processes.process="*clip.dll*" OR (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" AND Processes.process="*.dll,Main*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=rundll32.exe (Processes.process="*cred64.dll*" OR Processes.process="*clip64.dll*" OR Processes.process="*cred.dll*" OR Processes.process="*clip.dll*" OR (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*" AND Processes.process="*.dll,Main*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Amadey C2 check-in beacon to .php endpoint from AppData-resident process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Amadey's HTTP C2 registration/beacon: a process executing from AppData\Local\Temp or AppData\Roaming reaching a public .php endpoint (typically /index.php), and proxy URLs carrying the Amadey check-in signature (RC4+hex body prefixed 'r=' or plaintext id/vs/sd fields). Targets command_and_control per article Table 1. Rationale: Combines Amadey's documented execution location (AppData Temp/Roaming self-copy) with its C2 URI shape (/index.php) and the article Table 1 check-in fields id/vs/sd — plus the RC4+hex 'r=' body prefix confirmed by OALABS/Picus — for a proxy+endpoint pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/amadey-malware-explained-how-the-windows-botnet-loader-and-rat-work • https://research.openanalysis.net/cpp/stl/amadey/loader/config/2022/11/13/amadey.html • https://github.com/keithjjones/zeek-amadey-detector/blob/master/README.md
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate portable apps launched from AppData\Local\Temp contacting a vendor /index.php API
  • Browsers/updaters staged in AppData reaching .php web services
  • Proxy URLs with a benign 'r=' or 'id=' query parameter (analytics/redirectors)
  • Internal web apps served under /index.php over HTTP
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("microsoft.com","windowsupdate.com","mozilla.org","google.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary's full path/hash — Amadey runs as a random-named EXE in AppData\Local\Temp\<random>; validate signing and prevalence. Inspect the destination IP/domain reputation and whether the same host repeats the beacon on a fixed interval. 2) Contain: block the C2 IP/domain at the proxy/firewall and isolate the host; capture memory before reimaging to recover the RC4 key/config. 3) Hunt: pivot on the C2 IP across the fleet, look for rundll32 loading cred64.dll/clip64.dll on the same host (module deployment), and downstream identity abuse (impossible-travel sign-ins, MFA-bypass via stolen cookies) for accounts used on the device.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Roaming\\")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".php" or RemoteUrl has "index.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "index.php"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)[?&](r=[0-9a-f]{16,}|id=\d+&vs=|sd=[0-9a-f]{6})"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\* OR *\\appdata\\local\\temp\\* OR *\\appdata\\roaming\\*) @DestinationPort:(80 OR 443 OR 8080)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\AppData\\(Local\\Temp|Roaming)\\/i
| RemotePort=/^(80|443|8080)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*index.php*" (Web.url="*r=*" OR Web.http_method=POST) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*index.php*" (Web.url="*r=*" OR Web.http_method=POST) by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Amadey loader command handler spawning cmd/PowerShell from AppData self-copy AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Amadey's command handlers 0x0C (Execute CMD) and 0x0E (Execute PS1): a binary running from a randomly named AppData\Roaming or AppData\Local\Temp subfolder (Amadey self-copy) spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe to fetch and run downloaded payloads. Covers the loader's on-demand secondary-payload execution. Rationale: Anchors on Amadey's documented self-copy location (random-named subfolder of AppData\Local\Temp / AppData\Roaming, e.g. 406d6c22b040c6) as the parent of interpreter children, mapping article Table 2 handlers 0x0C/0x0E — tighter than generic temp-execution because of the hex/random folder regex. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/40483/ • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/36634/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/amadey-malware-explained-how-the-windows-botnet-loader-and-rat-work
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron/Squirrel and other per-user app updaters staged in AppData\Local\Temp spawning cmd/powershell
  • Software installers unpacking to a random AppData temp folder then calling PowerShell
  • Developer tooling (npm, pip, build caches) executing from AppData with random directory names
  • Browser/driver auto-updaters invoking cmd from AppData\Roaming
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("update.exe","squirrel.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe") or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","Google LLC","Mozilla Corporation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent EXE path/hash and the child command line — Amadey handlers typically fetch a URL then run it; look for download cradles (certutil, bitsadmin, Invoke-WebRequest, curl) or a dropped .exe in the same temp folder. Confirm the parent is unsigned and low-prevalence. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the parent binary and any dropped payloads, and block observed download/C2 destinations. 3) Hunt: on the same host check for rundll32 cred64.dll/clip64.dll loads and .php C2 beacons (sibling Amadey UCs), plus persistence (Run keys / scheduled tasks in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks pointing to the temp self-copy).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\(Roaming|Local\\Temp)\\[0-9A-Za-z]{6,}\\"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\(Roaming|Local\\Temp)\\[0-9A-Za-z]{6,}\\"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Amadey Loader Command Handler Spawning Script Interpreter from AppData
id: 2d7e9f01-5c3a-4b88-a1e2-6f7a8b9c0d1e
status: experimental

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:

level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SharkLoader / Cobalt Strike C2 egress to StrikeShark lookalike domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

SystemSettings.exe executing from non-standard path (SharkLoader DLL side-load host) AIInstallation High
Hunts the legitimate Windows binary SystemSettings.exe running from anywhere other than C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\ (or WinSxS). StrikeShark copies this signed binary to C:\ProgramData\, vendor-named decoy dirs (e.g. KasperskyLab), and %APPDATA%\xwreg / %APPDATA%\xgdf to side-load the malicious SystemSettings.dll (SharkLoader). The relocated binary is the launch point of the whole Cobalt Strike chain. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact relocation behaviour (copy SystemSettings.exe C:\ProgramData\, KasperskyLab/xwreg/xgdf decoy dirs). SystemSettings.exe only legitimately runs from ImmersiveControlPanel/WinSxS, making any other path near-deterministic for the side-load. Cross-checked against cybersecuritynews.com and cyberpress.org which confirm the SystemSettings.exe side-load and %APPDATA% working dirs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin manually copying SystemSettings.exe to a test/staging folder during Settings-app troubleshooting
  • Backup/imaging software shadowing the binary into a snapshot path that lacks the WinSxS marker
  • Security-product self-protection sandboxes that copy and re-execute system binaries
  • Application-virtualization layers (App-V/MSIX) that surface SystemSettings.exe from a redirected path
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and FolderPath has @"\ccmcache\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FolderPath, SHA256, and parent of the relocated SystemSettings.exe; confirm a SystemSettings.dll exists in the SAME directory (legit copies never carry that DLL beside them) and check for DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat siblings. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and quarantine the directory; block the C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com/.top, ms-tray.top) at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (w3wp/java) for the originating webshell, and sweep the fleet for SystemSettings.exe in ProgramData/AppData plus the dual schtasks persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\" and FolderPath !has @"\WinSxS\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\SystemSettings.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith @"C:\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\") and NewProcessName !has @"\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader encrypted payload files dropped (DscCoreR.mui + SyncRes.dat + SystemSettings.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of SharkLoader's distinctive component set in user-writable directories: the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll plus the encrypted in-memory-only modules DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish-decrypted) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128-decrypted API-hooking DLL). These filenames co-located in ProgramData/AppData are a near-unique campaign fingerprint. Rationale: Uses the article's exact module names DscCoreR.mui (Blowfish) and SyncRes.dat (AES-128) plus the side-loaded SystemSettings.dll — corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com describing the same DscCoreR.mui→SyncRes.dat decryption chain. DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat are non-Windows filenames so any user-writable occurrence is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party DSC (Desired State Configuration) tool legitimately staging a DscCore localized resource into ProgramData
  • Backup software re-hydrating an AppData folder that already contained the artifacts during a prior incident
  • Security-vendor sample-collection writing copies of these files into a quarantine/AppData path
  • Developer test fixtures that happen to reuse the SyncRes.dat name (rare)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe","sensendr.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether all three components landed in one directory; hash SystemSettings.dll and check signing — SharkLoader's DLL is unsigned/forged. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the directory, and capture a memory image (SyncRes.dat/Beacon are decrypted only in memory). 3) Hunt: pivot to the SystemSettings.exe process that loads the DLL, the schtasks persistence, and outbound beacons to the campaign C2 domains; sweep fleet for the same filename triad.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where not(FileName =~ "SystemSettings.dll" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\")
| summarize Components=make_set(FileName), Paths=make_set(FolderPath), DistinctComponents=dcount(FileName), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("SystemSettings.dll","DscCoreR.mui","SyncRes.dat")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| summarize Components=make_set(TargetFileName), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath), DistinctComponents=dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Web server process spawning command shell to relocate SystemSettings.exe (post-webshell staging) AIExploitation High
Hunts internet-facing server processes (w3wp.exe for Exchange/SharePoint, java for Openfire) spawning a child that references SystemSettings.exe — the article's webshell-driven post-exploitation step where the attacker copies SystemSettings.exe out of ImmersiveControlPanel to stage the SharkLoader side-load. Rationale: Pairs the article's named initial-access surfaces (Exchange/SharePoint=w3wp, Openfire=java) with the exact webshell command observed (copy SystemSettings.exe / cd ImmersiveControlPanel). A web-server parent referencing SystemSettings.exe is not a benign pattern. Confirmed by cyberpress.org listing Exchange/SharePoint/Openfire as exploited entry points. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom in-house web app that legitimately shells out to launch the Windows Settings UI (uncommon on a server)
  • Server administrators invoking SystemSettings via a management web console
  • Application pool running a deployment script that references a like-named internal tool
  • SCOM/monitoring agents reading the Settings binary path via w3wp-hosted health checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and the w3wp/java application pool identity; pull recent IIS/Openfire access logs for the source IP and the requested webshell URL just before the spawn. 2) Contain: take the public-facing app offline or block the source IP, isolate the server, and preserve the webshell file and w3wp memory. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of that web server over 30 days, locate the dropped SystemSettings.exe/.dll, and check for the CVEs named in the article (ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855, Openfire CVE-2023-32315, etc.) on the asset.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat9.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe","MSExchangeFrontEndTransport.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","tomcat","UMWorkerProcess.exe","MSExchangeFrontEndTransport.exe")
| where CommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader dropper masquerading as Cisco AnyConnect / Google Update installer AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the StrikeShark dropper executables that impersonate legitimate installers — GoogleUpdateStepup.exe, AutoUpdate.exe, and the AnyConnect predeploy lure — running from user-writable paths, and the decoy MSI written to %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi while SharkLoader is dropped silently elsewhere in %APPDATA%. Rationale: Uses the article's exact dropper filenames (GoogleUpdateStepup.exe — a non-genuine Google name; AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9) and the %APPDATA%\reports\AnyConnect-win-4.msi decoy path. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews.com and cryptika.com which name the Cisco AnyConnect and Google Update lures. AutoUpdate.exe is generic, hence the user-writable-path constraint and Medium confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/ • https://www.cryptika.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures-to-drop-sharkloader-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party application updaters genuinely named AutoUpdate.exe running from AppData (Spotify-style updaters)
  • A user re-running a real Cisco Secure Client predeploy installer from their Downloads folder
  • Portable apps shipping their own updater binary in %APPDATA%
  • Software-packaging test labs staging installers under Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "AutoUpdate.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropper and submit to VT/internal sandbox; check whether an MSI was written to %APPDATA%\reports\ and whether SharkLoader components (SystemSettings.dll/DscCoreR.mui/SyncRes.dat) appeared in a sibling %APPDATA% dir within seconds. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the dropper and any dropped MSI/DLLs, and reset the user's credentials. 3) Hunt: trace delivery (email/download referrer via FileOriginUrl), and fleet-sweep for the dropper hashes and the GoogleUpdateStepup.exe/AnyConnect predeploy names.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("GoogleUpdateStepup.exe","AutoUpdate.exe")) or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)AnyConnect-win-4\.10\.04071-predeploy-k9"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith @"\GoogleUpdateStepup.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\AutoUpdate.exe" or CommandLine has "AnyConnect-win-4.10.04071-predeploy-k9")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task persistence launching relocated SystemSettings.exe (SharkLoader) AIInstallation High
Hunts schtasks creation of a task whose action is the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe — SharkLoader's persistence, which the article/corroborators describe as a dual task set (one firing every 5 minutes for long-term persistence, one firing every second and self-deleting ~1.5s later for immediate launch). Rationale: Anchors on the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe being registered as a scheduled-task action — corroborated by cyberpress.org and cybersecuritynews.com, which document the dual 5-minute / 1-second self-deleting tasks executing the copied SystemSettings.exe from %APPDATA%\xwreg / xgdf. A scheduled task pointing at SystemSettings.exe is not a legitimate Windows pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cyberpress.org/sharkloader-targets-global-governments/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A management tool scripting a Settings-related scheduled task (essentially never references the raw exe)
  • Admin recreating a task during troubleshooting that copies the binary path
  • MDM/RMM agents registering display/settings maintenance tasks
  • Imaging/provisioning runs that template scheduled tasks
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML (schtasks /query /xml or Event 4698) — confirm the action path points to a non-ImmersiveControlPanel SystemSettings.exe and note the trigger cadence (5-min or 1-sec). 2) Contain: delete both tasks, kill the SystemSettings.exe process tree, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: locate the side-load directory the task launches from, recover SharkLoader components, and fleet-sweep DeviceProcessEvents/Event 4698 for any scheduled task whose action references SystemSettings.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "SystemSettings.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*SystemSettings.exe*" Processes.process="*/create*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | table firstTime dest user process parent_process_name count
SharkLoader / Cobalt Strike C2 egress to StrikeShark lookalike domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts connections or DNS to the StrikeShark C2 domains (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com, ms-record.top, ms-tray.top — Microsoft-lookalike infrastructure) and, behaviourally, the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe making outbound public connections from a non-Windows path (the Cobalt Strike beacon egress). Rationale: Uses the article's four C2 domains plus the corroborated behavioural anchor — a relocated SystemSettings.exe (the side-load/beacon host) making public egress. Note: the four domains are cited by the primary Kaspersky report; my second-source searches confirmed the SystemSettings.exe→Cobalt Strike beacon behaviour but did not independently re-list the domains, so the behavioural clause keeps the detection robust if the C2 rotates. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1574.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sandbox/malware-analysis VM detonating the sample and resolving the C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IOC domains
  • Typosquat-monitoring services resolving the lookalike domains for brand protection
  • A proxy/DNS-sinkhole appliance logging the lookup as it blocks it (benign block)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the connection/lookup (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) — if it's SystemSettings.exe from a non-Windows path, treat as confirmed beacon. 2) Contain: block all four domains and their resolved IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate the host, and capture memory for the in-memory Cobalt Strike beacon. 3) Hunt: pivot the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents for other beaconing hosts, correlate to the SystemSettings.exe side-load and schtasks persistence, and check the C2 IP for the internet-wide scanning behaviour the article attributes to it.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SystemSettings.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
cluw macOS stealer shell dropper fetching payload from ClawHavoc/AMOS C2 IP AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OpenClaw-skill prerequisite-block dropper: a macOS shell process (curl/bash/base64) whose command line references the cluw C2 at 2.26.75.16, the payload path /Xuvewuyur, or the persistent AMOS C2 at 91.92.242.30. This is the exact curl-pipe-bash delivery Unit 42 attributed to the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill. Rationale: Pins on three hard article IOCs (cluw C2 2.26.75.16, payload path /Xuvewuyur, AMOS C2 91.92.242.30) in shell command lines — the literal curl-pipe-bash prerequisite-block delivery. 91.92.242.30 cross-confirmed by ThreatFox + Trend Micro; 2.26.75.16//Xuvewuyur are Unit 42-original. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the tradingview-ai-indicator-assistant skill in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel team curling the C2 to capture the payload for analysis
  • Internal IR replay of the IOC during a tabletop exercise
  • Network-range coincidence: an unrelated internal host legitimately assigned 2.26.75.16 in a lab (verify it is the public C2, not RFC1918)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmware-tools","sandbox-agent") and DeviceName !startswith "MALWARE-LAB"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the matching process is on a macOS endpoint with OpenClaw installed; pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — the parent should be the OpenClaw agent/terminal, not a sandbox tool. 2) CONTAIN: Network-isolate the host, block 2.26.75.16 + 91.92.242.30 + the /Xuvewuyur URL at egress, and treat all credentials/API keys/keychain secrets reachable by the agent as compromised — force rotation. 3) HUNT: Search the same host and all OpenClaw users for the cluw hash (818aea61...), installed ClawHub skills published by the banned accounts, and any cron/LaunchAgent persistence pointing at the C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","bash","sh","zsh","base64","python","python3","osascript")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("2.26.75.16", "91.92.242.30", "/Xuvewuyur")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget","bash","base64","sh","python")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to ClawHavoc cluw / AMOS C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the cluw C2 (2.26.75.16) or the still-active AMOS dropper C2 (91.92.242.30) that distributes payloads via malicious OpenClaw/ClawHub skills. Pure IOC match independent of the delivery binary, so it catches second-stage beaconing the process-tree query may miss. Rationale: Direct match on the two campaign C2 IPs. 91.92.242.30 is corroborated as live AMOS infra by ThreatFox and Trend Micro three months after first disclosure; 2.26.75.16 is the newly-discovered cluw C2 from Unit 42 — any internal host reaching either is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/browse/malware/osx.amos/ • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel proxy or TI-platform sandbox actively polling the C2
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling fingerprinting the IP range
  • Lab VM detonating the cluw sample with live network
  • An internal asset coincidentally NATed behind a proxy that re-uses 2.26.75.16 as a public egress (verify ownership)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ti-sandbox","threatconnect-collector")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a shell/curl or the OpenClaw agent is malicious; a TI sandbox is benign. Confirm direction is outbound to the public C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics. Rotate any secrets the OpenClaw agent could reach (keychain, API tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the host for the cluw dropper command line, the 818aea61... hash, ClawHub skill installs, and cron/LaunchAgent persistence re-establishing the channel.

CommonSecurityLog

cluw infostealer and malicious ClawHub skill payload hashes on macOS AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the Unit 42 / Trend Micro file hashes for the malicious ClawHub skills or the cluw macOS infostealer are written or executed. Catches the payload regardless of which paste-site or C2 delivered it. Rationale: Exact-hash IOC sweep for the skill package (b6c7e0bf...) and cluw stealer (818aea61...) plus the four additional ClawHub skill hashes from the IOC set. Hashes are zero-FP by nature; the skill SHA256 is in both Unit 42 and Trend Micro's bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/content/dam/trendmicro/global/en/research/26/b/amos-stealer-openclaw/ioc-malicious-openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.txt • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/

  • Malware repository / VirusTotal mirror stored on an internal research host
  • Backup or DLP system snapshotting a host that already held the payload
  • Purple-team retaining the sample for detection-engineering tests
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "/Malware/" and DeviceName !startswith "SEC-RESEARCH"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash landed on a production macOS endpoint (not a malware-analysis host) and check FileOriginUrl/parent for the rentry.co or C2 source. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and rotate every secret the OpenClaw agent could access — keychain, API keys, SSH keys, crypto wallet keys. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all ClawHub skills installed by the user, look for Telegram Bot API exfil and cron/LaunchAgent persistence, and sweep the fleet for the same hashes and the C2 IPs.

OpenClaw paste-site (rentry.co/glot.io) curl-pipe-bash semantic-hijack dropper AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the ClawHavoc prerequisite-block lure pattern: a shell command line that fetches from a paste-site redirect (rentry.co/openclaw-code, glot.io) and pipes a Base64-decoded payload to a shell. Catches new variants that rotate C2 IPs but reuse the paste-site delivery, including the copy-paste-into-terminal lure. Rationale: Targets the durable behavioural pattern Unit 42, Koi and Trend Micro all describe (paste-site redirect lure + Base64-pipe-to-bash) rather than a single rotating IP, with the article-specific rentry.co/openclaw-code path as the high-fidelity anchor. Hunting tier because legit dev tooling also uses curl|bash one-liners. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/clawhavoc-341-malicious-clawedbot-skills-found-by-the-bot-they-were-targeting • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/b/openclaw-skills-used-to-distribute-atomic-macos-stealer.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a CLI tool via a documented rentry.co/glot.io curl|bash one-liner
  • CI/CD bootstrap script pulling a config snippet from glot.io
  • Homebrew/oh-my-zsh style install one-liners that pipe curl to bash (different domain but same shape if allowlist too broad)
  • Security-team replay of the lure during awareness training
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("brew","git") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("githubusercontent.com","brew.sh"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm the fetched paste-site is rentry.co/openclaw-code or another OpenClaw-themed slug, and that the parent is the OpenClaw agent or a terminal driven by it. Decode any inline Base64 to reveal the downstream URL/C2. 2) CONTAIN: If the decoded payload hits 2.26.75.16/91.92.242.30 or drops the cluw hash, isolate the host, block the paste-site path and C2, and rotate agent-reachable secrets. 3) HUNT: Inventory installed ClawHub skills for fake 'Prerequisites' blocks, and sweep for cron/LaunchAgent auto-updater persistence and Telegram Bot API exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rentry.co/openclaw-code", "rentry.co", "glot.io")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64", "| bash", "|bash", "| sh", "| zsh", "curl -", "-fsSL")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
