Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WhatsApp Desktop spawning WScript executing VBS from attachment Transfers dir · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin disabled (set to 0) by Windows Script Host · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A VBScript campaign distributed through WhatsApp deploying RMM software
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents · [LLM] Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory · [LLM] ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
WhatsApp Desktop spawning WScript executing VBS from attachment Transfers dir AIDelivery High
Hunts the campaign's initial-access foothold: WScript.exe launched directly by WhatsApp Desktop (WhatsApp.Root.exe) or executing a .vbs/.vbe from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers path. This is the exact process relationship Kaspersky documented confirming the financial-lure VBScript was run from the WhatsApp client. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim WhatsApp UWP package path (5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\...\Transfers) and parent WhatsApp.Root.exe from the article's process-tree analysis plus the .vbs/.vbe extension - a combination no benign workflow produces. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-uncovers-a-new-massive-campaign-spreading-malware-via-whatsapp
ATT&CKT1566 T1204.002 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate .vbs business automation a user genuinely received and ran via WhatsApp (rare in enterprise but possible in some SME workflows)
  • Security testing / red-team simulation of WhatsApp-delivered scripts
  • A user manually saving then double-clicking a benign VBS from chat (parent would be explorer.exe, not WhatsApp.Root.exe - reduces FP)
  • EDR/AV sandbox detonation of submitted samples on an analyst workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("devenv.exe","sense.exe") // exclude EDR sandbox/dev detonation hosts; tune to your analyst VLAN device group
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 of the VBS; check the file name against the campaign's financial-lure list (Financial Reports.vbs, Account Statement.vbs, Debt Statement.vbs, etc.) and look for the child wscript downloading to C:\Users\Public\Documents\. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the wscript.exe tree, and quarantine the VBS from the WhatsApp Transfers folder; reset the sending contact's WhatsApp session (account likely compromised). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same DeviceId for the working-dir creation under Public\Documents, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 registry write, and outbound connections to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "WhatsApp.Root.exe"
    or CommandLine has @"\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\"
| where CommandLine has_any (".vbs", ".vbe")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WhatsApp Desktop Spawning WScript Executing VBS Attachment
id: 6f3c1a2e-9b54-4f7d-8c21-2a1d6e0b4f10
description: Detects WScript/CScript launched by WhatsApp Desktop or executing a VBS/VBE from the WhatsApp UWP package Transfers directory, matching the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1566
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_parent_or_path:
    - ParentImage|endswith: '\WhatsApp.Root.exe'
    - CommandLine|contains: '\Packages\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\LocalState\Sessions\'
  selection_ext:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.vbs'
      - '.vbe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_parent_or_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) (@ParentImage:(*\\WhatsApp.Root.exe OR *\\whatsapp.root.exe) OR @CommandLine:*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*) @CommandLine:(*.vbs* OR *.vbe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ParentBaseFileName=/whatsapp\.root\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/\\Packages\\5319275A\.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\/i)
| CommandLine=/\.(vbs|vbe)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=wscript.exe OR Processes.process_name=cscript.exe) AND (Processes.parent_process_name="WhatsApp.Root.exe" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\5319275A.WhatsAppDesktop_cv1g1gvanyjgm\\LocalState\\Sessions\\*") AND (Processes.process="*.vbs*" OR Processes.process="*.vbe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
VBScript creating hidden working directory and VBS payloads under C:\Users\Public\Documents AIInstallation High
Hunts Stage 1 staging: WScript/CScript writing files into a randomized Temp_<random> or MSUpdate_<random> working directory under C:\Users\Public\Documents\, often flagged hidden+system. This is the campaign's payload-staging step prior to fetching the two secondary VBS scripts. Rationale: Uses the verbatim staging path C:\Users\Public\Documents\ plus the two documented randomized directory prefixes Temp_ and MSUpdate_, scoped to a wscript/cscript writer - benign software almost never drops VBS into Public\Documents under those name patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that legitimately stage VBS helpers in Public\Documents (uncommon, but check vendor)
  • IT logon-script tooling writing temp VBS to a shared public path
  • Backup/imaging software that names temp folders Temp_<id> (would not be a wscript writer - excluded by process filter)
  • Software installers using Public\Documents as a shared scratch area
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Veeam\", @"\Backup\")) // drop known backup scratch paths if they surface
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Enumerate the contents of the flagged Public\Documents working directory; capture any .vbs/.vbe and check for renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe (DLL-like names) inside it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, delete/quarantine the working directory, and kill the parent wscript tree. 3) HUNT: Tie the same DeviceId back to a WhatsApp.Root.exe -> wscript launch (UC1) and forward to ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry change and 202.61.160.0/24 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_") or TargetFileExtension in~ ("vbs","vbe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c2b9d7a1-4e83-49f6-b0a2-7d5c1e9f3a44

Renamed curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe running from Public\Documents working directory AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's LOLBin masquerading: curl.exe or bitsadmin.exe copied into the working directory and renamed with DLL-like filenames, exposed via the OriginalFileName-vs-FileName mismatch while executing from C:\Users\Public\Documents\. Used to download the secondary VBS payloads and the RMM ZIP. Rationale: Pivots on the article's documented trick of copying curl.exe/bitsadmin.exe under DLL-like names in the working dir - the PE OriginalFileName stays curl/bitsadmin while the on-disk FileName differs, a near-zero-FP masquerade signal when scoped to Public\Documents. Sentinel falls back to path+download-flag heuristics since 4688 lacks OriginalFileName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
ATT&CKT1036.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or admin manually copying curl.exe to a scratch dir and renaming it for testing
  • Portable-app launchers that bundle a renamed curl.exe
  • Software updaters shipping curl under a vendor-specific name (rarely in Public\Documents)
  • Sysmon OriginalFileName field unpopulated on very old binaries (causes misses, not FPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") // only keep LOLBins launched by the script host, dropping dev/admin manual copies
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the renamed binary's hash and full command line - extract the download URL it fetched (compare against 202.61.160.0/24, 38.55.151.63, baoxis.cc). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, quarantine the renamed LOLBin and any downloaded ZIP/VBS in the working dir. 3) HUNT: Look on the same host for the resulting UEMSAgent.msi/.mst install and the ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin registry write; sweep org for other hosts running curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Temp_", @"\MSUpdate_")
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://", "--url", "/transfer", "-o ", "--output")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Renamed curl/bitsadmin LOLBin Executing From Public Documents
id: a81e7c44-2f19-4c0b-9d6e-3b7a5e2c1f88
description: Detects curl.exe or bitsadmin.exe renamed (OriginalFileName/FileName mismatch) and executing from C:\Users\Public\Documents, the download mechanism in the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.003
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    OriginalFileName:
      - 'curl.exe'
      - 'bitsadmin.exe'
    Image|contains: '\Users\Public\Documents\'
  filter_realname:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_realname
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\* ) @OriginalFileName:(curl.exe OR bitsadmin.exe) -@Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\/i
| OriginalFilename=/^(curl|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\(curl|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, OriginalFilename, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.original_file_name=curl.exe OR Processes.original_file_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND NOT (Processes.process_name=curl.exe OR Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.original_file_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.original_file_name=curl.exe OR Processes.original_file_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND NOT (Processes.process_name=curl.exe OR Processes.process_name=bitsadmin.exe) AND Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.original_file_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin disabled (set to 0) by Windows Script Host AIExploitation High
Detects the Stage 2 'VBS script 1' behaviour: a script-host process writing HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin (or EnableLUA) to 0 to suppress admin elevation prompts. Scoped to wscript/cscript or a Public\Documents writer so it isolates the campaign's UAC-weakening step. Rationale: Uses the exact registry path from the article's Table 2 (HKLM\...\Policies\System\ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin) corroborated by SOCRadar's note that the value is set to 0, scoped to a script-host writer so legitimate GPO/admin UAC changes are excluded. Falcon left blank: UAC policy value is not an ASEP and is not reliably carried in AsepValueUpdate FDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
ATT&CKT1548.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GPO or Intune policy lowering UAC (initiating process would be svchost/gpsvc, not wscript - excluded)
  • Admin manually disabling UAC via a configuration script
  • Vendor installers that toggle UAC during setup (rare, and not script-host-driven)
  • Security baseline rollback tooling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","svchost.exe","taskhostw.exe") // exclude policy-driven UAC changes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writer is wscript/cscript and correlate with a Public\Documents working dir on the same host; re-enable UAC immediately (set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin back to 5, EnableLUA to 1). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, kill the script tree, and treat the host as elevated-compromise. 3) HUNT: Look for the follow-on UEMSAgent RMM install and any repeated ShellExecute runas elevation loops; sweep for the same registry write across the estate.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Policies\System"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin","EnableLUA")
| where RegistryValueData == "0"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAC ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin Disabled by Script Host
id: e4d2b6f0-7a31-4c98-bb15-9c0e2f7a83d2
description: Detects wscript/cscript setting ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin or EnableLUA to 0 under Policies\System, the UAC-weakening step in the WhatsApp VBScript RMM campaign.
references:

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\System*" AND (Registry.registry_value_name=ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin OR Registry.registry_value_name=EnableLUA) AND Registry.registry_value_data=0 by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Policies\\System*" AND (Registry.registry_value_name=ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin OR Registry.registry_value_name=EnableLUA) AND Registry.registry_value_data=0 by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beacon/download to WhatsApp-VBS campaign C2 infrastructure (202.61.160.0/24 + 38.55.151.63) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host connections to the campaign's attacker-controlled UEMS/management-server IPs and download domains. Confirmed by SOCRadar; the 202.61.160.x range overlaps prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infrastructure. Fires on any endpoint reaching these IOCs, with the initiating process surfaced for triage. Rationale: All six IPs are second-source-confirmed (SOCRadar lists the same 202.61.160.x management-server set plus 38.55.151.63, with 202.61.160.201 tied to prior ValleyRAT/Gh0st RAT infra). Domains are kept as has_any enrichment from the article's IOC list. CIDR 202.61.160.0/24 covers all five .160 hosts in one clause. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://www.technadu.com/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-installs-manageengine-rmm-kaspersky-warns/629801/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/analyst sandbox deliberately reaching the IOCs for study
  • Threat-intel scanning or proxy that proactively resolves IOC domains
  • Shared hosting reuse - 202.61.160.0/24 belongs to a provider that may also host benign sites (validate the exact host)
  • Legitimate use of oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com (Alibaba OSS) by unrelated apps - validate the full sdcwww subdomain before alerting on the domain clause
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63") // keep all IP hits; drop only browser hits to the shared-hosting Aliyun domain
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process - if it is wscript.exe, msiexec.exe, or a renamed curl/bitsadmin from Public\Documents, treat as confirmed; capture URL/port and bytes transferred. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IPs (and 202.61.160.0/24) and domains at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the host's process tree for the WhatsApp->wscript chain, the UEMS RMM install, and the UAC registry change; sweep all hosts that resolved the IOC domains.
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["temu.baskwms.top","invoice.msopsa.top","baoxis.cc","sdcwww.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["202.61.160.208","202.61.160.202","202.61.160.201","202.61.160.160","202.61.160.137","38.55.151.63"]);
let c2domains = dynamic(["temu.baskwms.top","invoice.msopsa.top","baoxis.cc","sdcwww.oss-ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (c2ips) or Url has_any (c2domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ManageEngine Endpoint Central (UEMS) agent silently installed as final RMM payload AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's end goal: deployment of a preconfigured ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent (UEMSAgent.msi + attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform + DCAgentServerInfo.json) giving covert remote access. Scoped to script-host / Public\Documents-spawned installs so it isolates abuse from legitimate enterprise Endpoint Central rollouts. Rationale: Anchors on the exact RMM artifact names UEMSAgent.msi, the attacker UEMSAgent.mst transform, and DCAgentServerInfo.json (ManageEngine Endpoint Central) confirmed by SOCRadar, gated on a script-host/Public\Documents context so legitimate sanctioned Endpoint Central deployments (pushed by your own server via SYSTEM/services) don't fire. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/ • https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-uses-fake.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned ManageEngine Endpoint Central agent rollout by your IT team (initiating process would be the EC server push / SYSTEM service, not wscript - the context gate excludes it)
  • Endpoint Central self-update writing agent files under Program Files (not Public\Documents)
  • An admin manually staging UEMSAgent.msi in a downloads/temp folder for testing
  • MSP-managed devices where Endpoint Central is the legitimate RMM (validate the management server in DCAgentServerInfo.json against your known UEMS server)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dcagentregister.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","services.exe") // exclude legitimate Endpoint Central self-managed agent file writes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open DCAgentServerInfo.json and the .mst transform - compare the configured management server against your sanctioned Endpoint Central server; if it points to 202.61.160.0/24 / 38.55.151.63 it is malicious. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate host, stop/uninstall the rogue UEMS agent and its service, kill active remote sessions, and block the management-server IPs. 3) HUNT: Trace back to the WhatsApp->wscript chain and UAC change on the host, and sweep the org for any UEMSAgent install whose server config is not your own.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("UEMSAgent.msi","UEMSAgent.mst","DCAgentServerInfo.json")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msiexec.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
    or FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "UEMSAgent" or CommandLine has "DCAgentServerInfo"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "cscript.exe" or CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7d3a1f56-0c92-4e84-a6b3-5f9e2c1d4b07
description: Detects creation of UEMSAgent.msi/UEMSAgent.mst/DCAgentServerInfo.json by a script host or from Public\Documents, the final RMM payload of the WhatsApp VBScript campaign.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/whatsapp-vbs-rmm-campaign/120290/
  - https://socradar.io/blog/whatsapp-vbscript-campaign-manageengine-endpoint/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_event

detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\UEMSAgent.msi'
      - '\UEMSAgent.mst'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\UEMSAgent.msi OR *\\UEMSAgent.mst OR *\\DCAgentServerInfo.json) (@Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe) OR @TargetFilename:*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(UEMSAgent\.(msi|mst)|DCAgentServerInfo\.json)$/i
| (ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|msiexec)\.exe$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=UEMSAgent.msi OR Filesystem.file_name=UEMSAgent.mst OR Filesystem.file_name=DCAgentServerInfo.json) AND (Filesystem.process_name=wscript.exe OR Filesystem.process_name=cscript.exe OR Filesystem.process_name=msiexec.exe OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

     | rename Processes.user as user]

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or SHA1 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e") or MD5 in~ ("c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c7f38cbb99c8b74fa0465293feeba700", "b7cd06c71465038b658a6dc1f273a507", "9f13c7b8ba391b2f597874e54d310648", "993f4c0cadbc769a4b0ed62a918db58d", "7f81c1bc8cfd588e8998968e2621456e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via repeated DELETE probing of /api/{realm}/alarm AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the enumeration stage of the removeAlarms IDOR: a single user or source IP firing many DELETE requests at the OpenRemote alarm endpoint with sequential auto-increment IDs, distinguishing existing vs non-existent alarms by 200 vs 404 responses. Article-specific because it keys on the exact DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm route and the sequential-ID probing behaviour described in the PoC. Rationale: Uses the exact DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm route and the article's 404-vs-200 presence-oracle behaviour over sequential IDs; a burst of DELETEs with mixed status codes from one principal is the enumeration fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190 T1087
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated integration/test suite exercising the alarm API against a staging realm
  • OpenRemote admin bulk-clearing stale alarms during maintenance
  • Monitoring/synthetic checks that create-and-delete alarms in a loop
  • Load-testing tooling replaying DELETE traffic
  • A legitimate alarm-retention job pruning many IDs at once
Suppression filter
| where csUsername != "-" and isnotempty(csUsername) and cIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the csUsername/cIP and confirm the account's home realm; check whether the deleted IDs span multiple realms (cross-tenant = confirmed exploit). Step 2 (contain): Disable the offending account/API token and block the source IP at the WAF; force OpenRemote upgrade to >= 1.24.2. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all DELETE /*/alarm requests from that principal over 30d, identify which victim realms lost alarms, and restore alarm records from backup where safety/security alerts were destroyed.

| where ReqCount > 15 and StatusVariety > 1   // 15 = burst threshold; >1 status = 200/404 presence-probing signature
| order by ReqCount desc

OpenRemote bulk alarm deletion — successful DELETE on /api/{realm}/alarm (removeAlarms IDOR) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the destructive action of GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf: an authenticated caller successfully invoking the bulk removeAlarms endpoint (HTTP DELETE on /api/{realm}/alarm) with a 200 response, permanently destroying alarm records. Article-specific because it targets the exact vulnerable route and verb from the PoC and scopes to successful (200) deletions rather than all traffic. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable route (DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm) and successful 200 status from the PoC, giving a direct signal for the destructive removeAlarms call rather than a generic technique template. OpenRemote cross-realm alarm deletion — user deletes alarms in a realm outside their baseline (IDOR priv-esc) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the core privilege-escalation step of the IDOR: an authenticated user issuing a successful DELETE against /api/{realm}/alarm for a realm they have never legitimately operated in. Builds a per-user baseline of accessed realms and flags first-time cross-realm deletions — directly modelling the article's 'authenticated user in any realm can delete alarms belonging to other realms'. Rationale: Extracts the realm from the article's /api/{realm}/alarm path and anti-joins each successful DELETE against the user's historically-accessed realms — a first-time cross-realm deletion is exactly the cross-tenant IDOR the advisory describes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine multi-realm administrator whose 14d baseline didn't yet include a rarely-used realm
  • New realm onboarded during the window so no baseline exists yet
  • Superuser/service account that legitimately spans all realms
  • Username casing/format differences causing baseline mismatch
  • Shared load-balancer or proxy collapsing csUsername to a service identity
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the flagged user's provisioned realm membership in OpenRemote's identity/ACL config; if the victim realm isn't assigned to them, the IDOR is confirmed. Step 2 (contain): Suspend the account and its tokens, upgrade to >= 1.24.2, and notify the victim tenant(s) that alarm records were destroyed. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP and any other accounts it authenticated, and enumerate every cross-realm DELETE to size the blast radius across tenants.

OpenRemote bulk alarm deletion by non-human / service account (stolen-credential scope escalation) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the scenario where a compromised service or bot account — which needs only authentication, not admin — is used to bulk-delete alarms via the removeAlarms IDOR. Flags DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm activity from accounts matching non-interactive/service naming, which should rarely if ever perform destructive alarm operations. Rationale: Combines the article's DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm route with a service-account name filter to catch stolen-credential abuse of the IDOR, since the vuln requires only authentication and service accounts performing bulk alarm deletes is anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf

  • Automation account performing scheduled alarm cleanup
  • Naming-convention overlap where a human account starts with 'api'
  • Monitoring bot that creates and deletes test alarms
  • Service account operating within a single, authorised realm
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Verify whether the service account is authorised to delete alarms and whether the targeted realm(s) match its intended scope; multi-realm deletions from one service identity indicate credential abuse. Step 2 (contain): Rotate the service account's credentials/API keys, restrict its role, and patch to >= 1.24.2. Step 3 (hunt): Trace where the service credential was used from (source IPs, other endpoints hit) to find the initial compromise and any additional cross-tenant impact.

Archive (TAR/ZIP) upload to Langflow BaseFileComponent file API (CVE-2026-55447 delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts POST uploads of tar/zip archives to Langflow's file-ingestion endpoints (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) that feed BaseFileComponent-derived nodes (Read File, Docling, Unstructured). This is the delivery vector for the symlink-TAR arbitrary-file-read in CVE-2026-55447, where a crafted archive is uploaded to a RAG ingestion flow. Rationale: Uses the article's named ingestion path (BaseFileComponent file upload) plus archive extensions; the endpoint strings /api/v1/files/upload and /api/v2/files are Langflow-specific upload routes that feed the vulnerable nodes. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/security-bulletin-path-traversal-vulnerability-file-processing-components-allows-unauthorized-file-system-access-and-potential-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading zipped document bundles into a RAG ingestion flow
  • Backup/export archives POSTed to the files API by an integration
  • Automated data-loader jobs bulk-uploading tar-packaged corpora
  • Security scanners / DAST tools probing the upload endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the uploaded archive from Langflow storage and inspect TAR members with `tar -tvf` — flag any entry whose type is symlink/hardlink or whose linkname is an absolute path (/etc, /root, /.ssh, secret_key). 2) Contain: if malicious members present, quarantine the archive, revoke the uploader's session/API token, and confirm Langflow is patched to >=1.9.2. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Langflow host and check whether the worker process subsequently read credential files (UC 'credential access') or made outbound connections (UC 'exfiltration').

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, FileName, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow worker reads JWT secret_key / OS credential files via symlink-TAR (CVE-2026-55447) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Langflow Python worker (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/langflow) opening sensitive files outside its working tree — the JWT secret_key file, /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws/credentials — which is the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-55447 that leads to JWT forgery and RCE. Rationale: Directly targets the article's exploit: the worker reading Langflow's secret_key (JWT signing secret) plus the reviewer-supplied credential paths (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws/credentials). A RAG worker opening /etc/shadow or a secret_key outside its config context is near-zero in normal operation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/security-bulletin-path-traversal-vulnerability-file-processing-components-allows-unauthorized-file-system-access-and-potential-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimately reading its OWN secret_key from LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR at startup (scope to reads of paths outside the config dir)
  • An operator's interactive python shell on the same host reading ~/.ssh for git/ssh ops
  • Backup agent running under the same service account touching /etc or /root
  • Config-management (Ansible/Salt) python modules reading /etc/passwd
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "secret_key" and FolderPath has_any ("/.cache/langflow/", "/app/langflow/", "/root/.cache/langflow/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the accessing PID is the Langflow web/worker process (not an admin shell) and that the accessed path is OUTSIDE Langflow's configured secret dir; check the ingested vector store for the leaked file contents. 2) Contain: rotate the Langflow secret_key (invalidates forged JWTs), force logout of all sessions, rotate any credentials the file exposed (SSH keys, AWS keys), and patch to >=1.9.2. 3) Hunt: search for anomalous JWT-authenticated flow creations (esp. Python Interpreter nodes) and for the RCE/exfil UCs on this host.

| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow Python worker spawns shell / network LOLBin (CVE-2026-55447 Python Interpreter node RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Langflow worker process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/langflow) spawning an interactive shell or network tool (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, socat). After JWT forgery, the CVE-2026-55447 chain achieves RCE via a Python Interpreter node whose payload shells out — a web/RAG worker parenting /bin/sh is highly anomalous. Rationale: Grounded in the article's stated RCE step — a Python Interpreter node running attacker code. A Langflow web/worker process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn) is not expected to fork shells or curl/nc; parent+child pairing turns generic execution into intent. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://gbhackers.com/langflow-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow components that legitimately shell out (e.g. a shell-command tool node an operator deliberately configured)
  • Container entrypoint/health-check scripts where uvicorn is PID1 and runs `sh -c`
  • python-based subprocess calls in custom components (e.g. calling `curl` for a webhook)
  • CI/agent tasks running under the same service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/healthcheck", "docker-entrypoint", "livenessProbe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line and the parent Langflow PID; determine if a Python Interpreter / shell-command node was recently added to a flow. 2) Contain: kill the child process tree, isolate the host, rotate the Langflow secret_key and any exposed credentials, and block outbound to any C2 the child contacted. 3) Hunt: enumerate all flows for Python Interpreter nodes with suspicious code, review who created/edited flows via the API (forged-JWT accounts), and check for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH authorized_keys) dropped by the child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|socat|perl|ruby)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow credential read followed by outbound egress within 5 min (CVE-2026-55447 exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a Langflow worker reading a sensitive credential/secret file with an outbound public network connection from the same worker within 5 minutes. Catches post-exploitation exfiltration of the stolen JWT secret_key or OS credentials in the CVE-2026-55447 chain. Rationale: Chains the article's two decisive artifacts — the worker reading secret_key/OS credentials and then egressing — inside a tight 5-minute window, which the reviewer flagged as the missing post-exploitation context. The temporal + same-host + same-process-family join keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://cyberpress.org/langflow-ai-pipeline-rce-exploited/
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimately reading its own secret_key at startup then making outbound LLM/API calls (OpenAI, vector DB) within 5 min
  • Backup agent reading /etc or ~/.ssh then uploading to cloud storage
  • Telemetry/update agent under same account phoning home post config-read
  • A RAG flow that reads an allow-listed local doc and calls an external embedding API
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("openai.com", "anthropic.com", "cohere.ai", "pinecone.io", "huggingface.co")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the read path is genuinely out-of-scope (not Langflow's own config secret_key) and that the outbound IP is not a known LLM/vector-DB provider; capture bytes-out. 2) Contain: block the destination IP/domain, isolate the host, rotate secret_key and all exposed credentials, and revoke active JWT sessions. 3) Hunt: review the vector store for leaked file content, enumerate other hosts running <1.9.2 Langflow, and check for inbound flow-creation from forged-JWT sessions.

Langflow worker creates symlink in temp dir during TAR extraction (CVE-2026-55447 traversal setup) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the Langflow worker creating symbolic links / files in /tmp or /var/tmp during BaseFileComponent TAR extraction — the actual _unpack_bundle attack step where a malicious tar's symlink member is written to disk pointing at an out-of-tree credential path before process_files() reads the target. Rationale: Implements the reviewer's traversal-setup hypothesis using the article's _unpack_bundle mechanism: the worker writes tar members into a temp extraction dir; auditd symlink syscalls are the accurate telemetry, with DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten as best-effort where symlink syscall logging is absent. Names/'..' filter narrows to credential-targeting members. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75
ATT&CKT1083 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate document bundles that happen to contain files named 'credentials.docx' or similar
  • python-based build/test tooling writing scratch files to /tmp
  • Antivirus or backup software staging files in /var/tmp
  • Application caches or session temp files created by the same worker
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/pip-", "/tmp/tmp", "/var/tmp/systemd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the created temp file and check whether it is a symlink (`ls -l`) and where its target points; correlate with a preceding archive upload (UC 'archive upload'). 2) Contain: if it symlinks to a credential path, quarantine the source archive, kill the worker if mid-exploit, and patch to >=1.9.2 (which rejects symlink/hardlink tar members). 3) Hunt: check whether the symlink target was subsequently read (UC 'credential access') and whether egress followed (UC 'exfiltration'); audit all recent uploads to BaseFileComponent flows.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|langflow)$"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(passwd|shadow|id_rsa|credentials|secret_key)" or FolderPath has ".."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "type=SYSCALL"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("syscall=symlink", "syscall=symlinkat")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("python", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "langflow")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Langflow flow-ID harvesting via burst GET /api/v1/flows enumeration · [LLM] Langflow instances exposed to CVE-2026-55255 (version < 1.9.1) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow IDOR exploitation via repeated POST /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) · [LLM] Langflow recon-to-exploit chain: flow enumeration then /api/v1/responses from same source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Langflow flow-ID harvesting via burst GET /api/v1/flows enumeration AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single client rapidly enumerating the Langflow flow API (/api/v1/flows*) to collect valid flow UUIDs — the reconnaissance step that precedes CVE-2026-55255 IDOR exploitation. Article-specific because it keys on the exact Langflow flow-listing/read API paths the attacker walks before abusing /api/v1/responses. Rationale: Uses the exact Langflow flow API path family (/api/v1/flows*) that the corroborated Sysdig/Mallory writeup shows the attacker enumerating to collect valid UUIDs before IDOR replay; volumetric per-source threshold catches harvesting that individual requests wouldn't. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef684-a9a6-79cd-b1c7-47a36cffec6e
ATT&CKT1526 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user/admin opening many flows in the Langflow UI (each open = a flow GET)
  • CI/CD or IaC automation that lists and validates flows on every deploy
  • Monitoring/health-check job polling the flows API on a schedule
  • A dashboard or embedded app auto-refreshing the flow list frequently
  • Bulk import/export of flows by a legitimate operator
Suppression filter
| where csUsername !in ("svc-langflow-ci","svc-monitoring") and cIP !in ("10.10.0.0")   // replace with your automation accounts / internal orchestration IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the cIP/csUsername is not a known internal automation or admin. Check whether the flow API reads span UUIDs the principal does not own (join against Langflow flow-ownership export if available). 2) CONTAIN: If unowned flows were read, revoke the offending Langflow API key (x-api-key) and block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy; force key rotation. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same cIP/key to POST /api/v1/responses and /api/v1/run* activity (UC2/UC3) and to any /api/v1/validate/code calls (chained RCE, CVE-2025-3248) within the following minutes.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/flows"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctFlowPaths = dcount(csUriStem), Methods = make_set(csMethod), Statuses = make_set(scStatus), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, csUsername, sSiteName
| where RequestCount >= 30 or DistinctFlowPaths >= 15   // burst of flow-API reads = UUID harvesting; tune per legit UI usage
| order by RequestCount desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 30 OR distinct_flow_paths >= 15
| eval firstSeen=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastSeen=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_flow_paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/flows*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/flows*") by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest

Langflow IDOR exploitation via repeated POST /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single client (IP or API key) invoking the vulnerable Langflow /api/v1/responses endpoint many times — the CVE-2026-55255 IDOR that executes another user's flow by supplying its UUID. Article-specific: the endpoint, method, and the 200/404 outcome pattern come straight from the advisory PoC and the fix's 404-oracle note. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable route (POST /api/v1/responses) named in the advisory and its 200-vs-404 outcome oracle (the fix explicitly changed cross-user lookups to 404); a per-principal repetition threshold separates IDOR abuse from a single legitimate call. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate OpenAI-compatible client/integration that heavily uses the /api/v1/responses shim
  • Chatbot or app frontend making many flow-execution calls for real users
  • Load/perf testing against the responses endpoint
  • A batch job that executes the same owned flow repeatedly
  • Automated regression tests replaying responses calls after a deploy
Suppression filter
| where csUsername !in ("svc-langflow-app","svc-chatbot") and cIP !in ("10.20.0.0")   // replace with legitimate integration accounts / app-tier IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the 200 responses correspond to flows the calling principal actually owns (correlate the x-api-key/user to flow ownership). A mix of 404 (cross-user misses) then 200 strongly indicates IDOR success. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the API key, block the source IP, and upgrade Langflow to >= 1.9.1 immediately if still < 1.9.1. 3) HUNT: Review flows executed for secret-leaking prompts (e.g., input 'leak api keys'), rotate any credentials referenced by the victim flows, and check for follow-on /api/v1/validate/code calls (chained RCE).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/v1/responses"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| summarize InvocationCount = count(), StatusSet = make_set(scStatus), Success200 = countif(scStatus == 200), NotFound404 = countif(scStatus == 404), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, csUsername, sSiteName
| where InvocationCount >= 10   // repeated IDOR-endpoint invocation from one principal; 404s = cross-user misses on patched hosts, 200s = hits
| order by InvocationCount desc

Langflow recon-to-exploit chain: flow enumeration then /api/v1/responses from same source AIExploitation High
High-fidelity correlation of the observed CVE-2026-55255 campaign: the same client first enumerates flows (/api/v1/flows*) to harvest UUIDs, then replays them into POST /api/v1/responses. The two-endpoint sequence from one source within a short window is far more specific than either signal alone. Rationale: Reproduces the exact two-step campaign chain documented by Sysdig/Mallory (query /api/v1/flows/ to collect UUIDs, then POST them to /api/v1/responses) as a same-source, recon-before-exploit correlation — the highest-fidelity, lowest-FP expression of this IDOR. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019ef684-a9a6-79cd-b1c7-47a36cffec6e • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/

  • CI pipeline that lists and then test-executes flows it created
Suppression filter

1) TRIAGE: The recon+exploit sequence from one source is rarely benign — confirm the principal is not a sanctioned orchestrator, and check whether executed flow UUIDs belong to other users. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the API key, block the IP, and patch to Langflow >= 1.9.1. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every flow UUID this source touched, notify those flow owners, rotate secrets/keys those flows reference, and look for exfil of flow outputs or subsequent /api/v1/validate/code (RCE) and /api/v2/workflow calls from the same source.

Langflow instances exposed to CVE-2026-55255 (version < 1.9.1) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces onboarded hosts running a Langflow version affected by CVE-2026-55255 (pip:langflow < 1.9.1) so they can be prioritised for the 1.9.1 upgrade before the IDOR is exploited. Attack-surface / exposure detection, not behavioural. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE id (CVE-2026-55255) and the advisory's stated affected range (pip:langflow < 1.9.1, fixed in 1.9.1) against Defender TVM; internet-facing enrichment prioritises the hosts an authenticated attacker can actually reach. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2

Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Isolated dev/test Langflow not reachable by untrusted authenticated users
  • A decommissioned instance still in the software inventory
  • TVM lag reporting a version already upgraded to 1.9.1
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Langflow version is genuinely < 1.9.1 and whether the host is internet-facing or reachable by non-admin authenticated users. 2) CONTAIN: Schedule/enforce upgrade to Langflow >= 1.9.1; if immediate patch isn't possible, restrict /api/v1/responses, /api/v1/run*, and /api/v2/workflow to trusted principals at the proxy. 3) HUNT: On any confirmed-vulnerable host, retro-hunt UC1–UC3 web-log detections over the exposure window to determine whether the IDOR was already exploited.

Craft CMS resource-js Host/X-Forwarded-Host poisoning (CVE-2026-55791) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts unauthenticated requests to Craft's /actions/app/resource-js endpoint where a single client cycles multiple distinct Host header values, the fingerprint of trustedHosts:['any'] abuse poisoning $baseUrl. Article-specific: only this endpoint reflects attacker-controlled content as application/javascript. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable URI 'app/resource-js' and the article's stated mechanism of poisoning the Host header to manipulate $baseUrl; dcount(Host) per client avoids needing the victim's domain (no placeholder) while flagging the header-rewriting pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-domain Craft install serving several front-end hostnames from one CDN/proxy egress IP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors probing the site with varied Host headers
  • Security scanners (Burp, Nuclei) run by the org's own pentest team
  • Shared NAT egress where many real users appear as one SrcIpAddr
  • CDN revalidation requests carrying origin-shield Host values
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !in ("monitoring.internal")  // append known synthetic-monitor egress hosts after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull HostSamples for the flagged SrcIpAddr — confirm values are IP literals, internal names, or attacker domains rather than the site's real hostnames; check response status/size on those requests. 2) Contain: in config/general.php set trustedHosts to the explicit allowed host(s) and upgrade craftcms/cms to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15; block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC for outbound fetches from the web-server process and to admin plugin-install POSTs from the same window.
let lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "resource-js"
| extend HostHeader = tostring(HttpHostName)
| where isnotempty(HostHeader)
| summarize DistinctHosts = dcount(HostHeader), HostSamples = make_set(HostHeader, 10), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctHosts > 3   // one client cycling >3 distinct Host values at resource-js = header fuzzing / baseUrl poisoning
| order by DistinctHosts desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Web.http_host) as distinct_hosts, values(Web.http_host) as host_values, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*app/resource-js*" OR Web.url="*action=app/resource-js*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_hosts > 3 | sort - distinct_hosts
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.http_host) as distinct_hosts, values(Web.http_host) as host_values, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*app/resource-js*" OR Web.url="*action=app/resource-js*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_hosts > 3 | sort - distinct_hosts
Craft CMS trustedHosts bypass via localhost/127.0.0.1 Host header from external IP AIDelivery Medium
Detects requests to Craft's resource-js endpoint where the Host or X-Forwarded-Host header claims to be localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 but the source IP is public — a direct attempt to defeat front-end Host validation against the trustedHosts:['any'] default. Single occurrence is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoint plus the concrete loopback literals attackers supply to spoof a trusted origin; pairing a loopback Host with a public source IP is behaviour no legitimate client produces, making it a low-FP alerting candidate. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/
ATT&CKT1190 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal health-check that wrongly egresses through a public IP while sending Host: localhost
  • Misconfigured reverse proxy forwarding a literal localhost Host upstream
  • Container-to-container probe traversing a public NAT
  • Pentest/scanner deliberately fuzzing Host headers
  • Load balancer health probe rewritten to 127.0.0.1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SrcIpAddr is genuinely external and not an internal monitor NAT'd to a public address; review HTTP status/size of the response. 2) Contain: set explicit trustedHosts in config/general.php, upgrade craftcms/cms to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: check for outbound fetches from php-fpm/nginx to internal or metadata IPs and for any /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin POSTs in the following minutes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "resource-js"
| extend HostHeader = tolower(tostring(HttpHostName))
| where HostHeader has_any ("localhost","127.0.0.1","[::1]","::1","0.0.0.0")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and SrcIpAddr !in ("::1","127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Blind SSRF: Craft web-server process fetching internal/cloud-metadata hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF half of CVE-2026-55791 — Craft's Guzzle client (running under php-fpm/nginx/httpd) making outbound connections to RFC1918, link-local, or the 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata endpoint after $baseUrl poisoning. Article-specific: the vuln forces this Guzzle fetch with ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true. Rationale: Targets the article's stated server-side fetch (Craft::createGuzzleClient()->get($url)) by pivoting on the web-server process making unexpected internal/metadata connections; the 169.254.169.254 focus is corroborated by Craft's related metadata-SSRF CVE-2026-27129, and DB ports are excluded to suppress routine backend traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-27129/

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • nginx reverse-proxying to an internal app server
  • Legitimate use of an internal package mirror or Composer proxy
  • App-level health checks hitting internal services
  • Sidecar/service-mesh proxies on private IPs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "10." and RemotePort == 9200)  // example: drop known internal Elasticsearch; extend with allowed internal services after baselining
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and the InitiatingProcessId — was 169.254.169.254 or an internal admin port hit, and is there a matching resource-js request in web logs? 2) Contain: rotate any cloud IAM credentials reachable via metadata if 169.254.169.254 was contacted, set explicit trustedHosts, and patch craftcms/cms. 3) Hunt: review web logs for resource-js Host poisoning from the originating window and for outbound connections to attacker-owned public IPs reflecting fetched JS.

Craft CMS 1-click RCE: plugin-install POST riding a poisoned resource-js JS load AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the cache-poisoning payoff of CVE-2026-55791 — an admin browser that loaded the resource-js response as application/javascript then, within minutes from the same client, POSTs to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin (session riding using window.Craft.csrfTokenValue). This is the RCE step, not a generic CSRF check. Rationale: Uses the two concrete article URIs ('resource-js' returning application/javascript, and 'actions/plugins/install-plugin' POST) plus the same-client temporal link the cache-poisoning-to-session-riding chain requires; plugin install is a rare CP action so the correlation is high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh/
ATT&CKT1185 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Automated CI/deploy tooling that installs plugins via the CP from a fixed IP
  • Penetration test reproducing the chain
  • Admin behind same NAT as the resource-js request during routine work
  • Plugin Store updates triggering install-plugin during a CP session
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "CraftDeployBot"  // exclude known CI deploy automation user-agent after confirming it
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the resource-js response served to that client was attacker-controlled (external Host header, unexpected size/hash) versus the legitimate cached asset; identify the admin account tied to the session. 2) Contain: disable/inspect the installed plugin, force-logout and rotate the admin session + CSRF, set explicit trustedHosts, and patch to >=4.17.9 / >=5.9.15. 3) Hunt: review the file system for newly written plugin/PHP files and the web-server process for child processes or outbound C2 following the install.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Crossplane package installed by mutable tag instead of immutable digest AIInstallation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit logs for pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function installs whose spec.package references a version tag rather than an @sha256 digest. This is the exact precondition GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r requires: when a package is pulled by tag, a malicious/compromised OCI registry can serve a correctly-signed image for cosign verification and then swap in unsigned content for the actual pull. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's stated exploit precondition #2 ('Install packages using tag references rather than digests'). The detection keys on the real Crossplane API (pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function, spec.package) and the digest sentinel '@sha256:' that the fix mandates; absence of the digest is exactly what makes an install TOCTOU-exposed. Corroborated against the GHSA, the GitLab advisory mirror, and Crossplane's ImageConfig/package docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/crossplane/crossplane/v2/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r/ • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps/Argo/Flux pipelines that pin Crossplane packages to a semantic-version tag (e.g. provider-aws:v1.20.0) rather than a digest — common and benign in many shops
  • Platform-team installs from the org's own trusted internal registry where tag mutability is acceptable
  • Dev/sandbox clusters where engineers iterate on packages by floating tag
  • Initial cluster bootstrap installing first-party Upbound/Crossplane marketplace packages by tag
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style bots bumping a package tag during routine upgrades
Suppression filter
| where not (PackageRef startswith "xpkg.upbound.io/upbound/" or PackageRef startswith "xpkg.crossplane.io/")   // keep third-party / org-uncontrolled registries (advisory precondition #3), drop trusted first-party marketplace
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending Provider/Configuration object and its spec.package. Confirm whether the registry host is one the org controls (advisory precondition #3) and whether an ImageConfig with cosign verification matches that image. A tag-pinned package from a third-party registry under cosign verification is the high-risk case. 2) Contain: re-pin the package to the resolved immutable digest (spec.package: repo@sha256:...) and ensure Crossplane is on a fixed build (v2.3.3 / v2.2.3 or later); for vulnerable builds, prefer digest references org-wide until upgraded. 3) Hunt: inventory all pkg.crossplane.io resources still on tags, review the installed package revisions' Verified condition for skipped/incomplete status, and check whether the registry served differing digests for verify vs pull around the install time.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update", "patch")
| extend ObjRef = todynamic(ObjectRef)
| where tostring(ObjRef.apiGroup) == "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where tostring(ObjRef.resource) in ("providers", "configurations", "functions")
| extend ReqObj = todynamic(RequestObject)
| extend PackageRef = tostring(ReqObj.spec.package)
| where isnotempty(PackageRef) and PackageRef !contains "@sha256:"   // not digest-pinned => mutable tag => TOCTOU-exposed
| extend Actor = tostring(todynamic(User).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, Kind = tostring(ObjRef.resource), ObjectName = tostring(ObjRef.name), PackageRef, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7a3c1e8b-2f4d-4c9a-b6e1-9d2f5a1c3e47
description: Detects creation/update of a Crossplane Provider, Configuration or Function whose spec.package uses a mutable tag rather than an immutable @sha256 digest, the precondition for the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r signature-verification TOCTOU.
references:

  - https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/
